extracted.intended_audience: general readers, genealogists, family historians, and people creating or studying family trees
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on representing family relationships as charts (ancestral, descendant, pedigree, genogram) including common formats, numbering systems, layout conventions, and modelling considerations for genealogy and related fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation conventions (generation layout and orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Family trees are often presented with the oldest generations at the top of the tree and the younger generations at the bottom. In some ancestry charts, an individual appears on the left and their ancestors appear to the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a consistent orientation: classic top-to-bottom for multi-generation trees; left-to-right for some ancestry charts. Be aware that different layouts change visual emphasis (e.g., ancestry charts appear wider at the top, descendant charts are narrowest at the top).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancestral chart vs descendant chart distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: An ancestry chart is a tree showing the ancestors of an individual and not all members of a family; a descendant chart depicts all the descendants of an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the chart type based on purpose: use an ancestral chart when tracing an individual's forebears (wider at top), and a descendant chart when documenting all descendants (narrower at top).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ahnentafel (genealogical numbering system) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An ahnentafel is a genealogical numbering system listing a person's direct ancestors in a fixed sequence: Subject (proband), Father, Mother, Paternal grandfather, Paternal grandmother, Maternal grandfather, Maternal grandmother, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbering rules: apart from the subject, all even-numbered persons are male and all odd-numbered persons are female; a person's father's number is double the person's number, and the mother's number is double the person's number plus one. The system can also be displayed as a tree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan chart format
rubrics_metrics.description: A fan chart features a half circle chart with concentric rings: the subject is the inner circle, the second circle is divided in two (each side is one parent), the third circle is divided in four, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fan charts to depict paternal and maternal ancestors compactly; each concentric ring represents another generation, making the chart useful for visual summaries of ancestry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-scale and chronological plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage of time can be included to illustrate ancestry and descent; a time scale is often used, expanding radially across the center, divided into decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including time, plot names at their birth year on the time scale, place children on branches around the centre, and join spouses' names to children's names. Using time helps show generational spacing and historical context (e.g., great-grandparents in the centre to portray four or five generations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of nuclear families and spouses
rubrics_metrics.description: Nuclear families of parents and children branch off to grandchildren; spouses' names join children's names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent parent–child units as branches; explicitly connect spouses to indicate partnerships and to trace descent through family units rather than only bloodlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-theory modelling (trees vs directed acyclic graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: While family trees are depicted as trees, family relations do not in general form a tree in the strict sense of graph theory because distant relatives can mate. However, because a parent must be born before their child, ancestry forms a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Matrilineal and patrilineal descent graphs (mother–daughter or father–son relationships) can form trees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model genealogical data recognizing potential merges (common ancestors) that violate strict tree structure; choose a DAG-aware representation or simplify to lineages (matrilineal/patrilineal) when appropriate. Expect descendant charts to have irregular structure since individuals may have variable numbers of children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of genograms for medical and social-work detail
rubrics_metrics.description: More detailed family trees, used in medicine and social work, are known as genograms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use genograms when additional family information (medical history, social relationships, behavioral patterns) is required beyond basic pedigree structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative grouping approaches (surname or office holders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some family trees might include all members of a particular surname (e.g., male-line descendants) or all holders of a certain office, such as the Kings of Germany, which represents the reliance on marriage to link dynasties together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose grouping rules (surname-based, office-based, male-line only) depending on research goals; document any selection biases (e.g., excluding female-line descendants) so users understand scope and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and historical variation in genealogical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Representations and record-keeping of genealogies vary across cultures and time: some cultures used oral traditions (griots), others maintained written dynastic pedigrees or traced legendary descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt representation and interpretation to cultural context; be cautious about mythological or legendary claims and annotate or source them appropriately. Recognize that continuity and completeness of records differ widely by region and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy considerations for living family trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy should be considered when preparing a living family tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting living individuals, follow privacy best practices: obtain consent, limit sensitive data exposure, and consider omitting or anonymizing living persons to protect personal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting and citing genealogical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Genealogical claims (especially long lineages or historic claims) require documentation and reliable sources; many sections and historical statements note the need for citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support pedigree assertions with citations to primary records or reputable secondary sources; flag unsourced material and be transparent about evidential strength and gaps.
